Recent Changes · Review Details page

Recent Changes shows
field-level edits.

During a review, people edit answers across teams and time zones. Recent Changes shows field-level edits — who changed what, when, and from what.

Real-time sync · field-level history · burst grouping

The one rule

field_versions holds the current value; field_version_events holds every accepted value in between. Grouping happens only in the UI, never in storage.

New to this feed? open a plain-English definition.

The feed — field-level changes in time order, searchable by question, filterable by answer type and pillar

Checklist popover — current state + per-item diff badges

Intermediate trail — burst history collapsed behind one grouped row

The mental model: field_versions stores the current answer. field_version_events preserves the recent trail. The UI groups adjacent edits from the same actor within a , but storage keeps every accepted step until retention expires.

01 · The problem

Why historical values were lost

The sync system kept only the latest value in field_versions. Old events pulled from the server carried the current value, not the historical value they originally represented.

A fresh browser syncing for the first time saw Yes, Yes, Yes instead of Yes, No, Yes — the sequence was lost on every pull, so teams could not audit or debug conflicting edits.

server event stream (time →)
evt-1  answer = Yes
evt-2  answer = No      ← lost: overwritten by latest value
evt-3  answer = Yes     ← also lost

fresh client pull → sees [Yes, Yes, Yes]
02 · Attempts

Why earlier approaches failed

Earlier attempts mixed up current state, history, and presentation — the final design keeps them separate.

03 · End to end

The same payload, one added write

The client still pushes the normal sync event shape with fields[]. The server accepts the event, writes event metadata, and inserts one field_version_events row per accepted field inside the same Postgres transaction.

04 · Interaction

How burst grouping works

Rapid edits from one actor within five seconds are grouped into a single row. Play the simulation to see how accepted events map to the Recent Changes feed — the checklist case shows item swaps that look identical by count alone.

Accepted field history
Recent Changes row
05 · Storage

Two tables, two jobs

field_versions stays compact because it is one row per field. field_version_events is high-churn by design, so it must be retained only as long as it is useful for Recent Changes and replay.

If Bob changes security-q-1 from No to Yes, the current table ends with just Yes — the history table gets a row like this.

field_version_events record
{
  "id": "fve_8f2a1c",
  "event_id": "evt_7d391a",
  "entity_type": "review_answer",
  "entity_id": "rev-7:security-q-1",
  "field_name": "answer",
  "previous_value": "No",
  "value": "Yes",
  "hlc": "2026-06-04T10:00:01.120Z:0002:actor_bob",
  "actor_id": "actor_bob",
  "updated_at": "2026-06-04T10:00:01.120Z"
}
06 · What's next

Local TTL ships. The server policy is still open.

Raw field history should not compete with attachments, templates, or audit records for storage. A 14-day client-side sweep now prunes old events and field_version_events rows after sync or at startup — the filter bar shows a Last 14 days notice near that boundary.

Still open: a durable, server-side retention policy — window length, batched sweeps, metrics, and pull-safety tests. That needs its own engineering design discussion.

Open engineering design discussion →

The feed is a display convenience. The source of truth is still two tables and one grouping rule.
